stemMd:
Archaeologists have long assumed that the stone towers scattered across the hills of the Kaldera plateau were built for defense: they are tall and thick-walled, and they stand on high ground. Archaeologist Mariam Toussaint points out that defense does not explain where the towers are. Many stand on slopes facing away from the valley routes that any attacker would have used, and few are within sight of one another, as towers would need to be to pass warnings along. What nearly every tower does overlook, Toussaint found, is a spring or a seasonal stream. She proposes that the towers were built to mark communities' claims to water, a resource scarce enough on the dry plateau to justify such a large investment of labor.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The towers on the Kaldera plateau were too poorly built to have withstood an attack by an organized force.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Communities on the Kaldera plateau used their towers mainly to send warnings to one another about approaching attackers.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Toussaint argues that where the Kaldera towers stand is better explained by a link to water than by a defensive purpose.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Toussaint has shown that the communities of the Kaldera plateau never faced any threat of attack from outside.

explanationMd:
Texts that open with "have long assumed" usually go on to challenge the assumption, and the main idea is the challenge. Here the assumption is that the towers were defensive. Toussaint's argument rests on the towers' **locations**: many face away from the routes attackers would use, and few can see each other, so they could not relay warnings. What they do share is a view of a spring or stream, which leads to her proposal that they marked claims to water.

The choice saying that Toussaint explains the towers' positions by a link to water rather than by defense captures both the old view being challenged and the new one she offers.

Check the strongest-sounding wrong answer, that the plateau never faced attack. Toussaint argues only that defense does not explain where the towers stand; she makes no claim about whether attacks ever happened, so that choice says far more than the text does.

distractorRationale.a: The text says the towers are tall and thick-walled, which is why defense seemed plausible. Toussaint's objection is about where they stand, not about how well they were built.
distractorRationale.b: This is the role the text argues against. Few towers are within sight of one another, which the text says they would need to be in order to pass warnings along.
distractorRationale.d: This overstates Toussaint's argument. She claims that defense does not explain the towers' locations, not that the communities were never threatened.

accessibilityText: A short archaeology passage. Archaeologists have long assumed that the stone towers on the hills of the Kaldera plateau were defensive, because they are tall, thick-walled and on high ground. Archaeologist Mariam Toussaint points out that defense does not explain where they are: many face away from the valley routes attackers would use, and few are within sight of one another, as they would need to be to pass warnings. Nearly every tower overlooks a spring or a seasonal stream, and she proposes that the towers marked communities' claims to water, which was scarce on the dry plateau. The question asks for the main idea. The choices are: the towers were too poorly built to withstand an organized attack; communities used the towers mainly to send warnings about approaching attackers; Toussaint argues that where the towers stand is better explained by a link to water than by a defensive purpose; and Toussaint has shown that the communities never faced any threat of attack.

provenance.notes: Original main-idea item. The Kaldera plateau, its towers and Toussaint's argument are invented; the strongest distractor overstates the scope of her claim.

review.author: sat-wave8-rw-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The text contrasts the defense assumption with Toussaint's finding that tower locations track springs/streams, so she argues location is better explained by water claims. 'Poorly built' contradicts 'tall and thick-walled'; 'sending warnings' is undercut by towers not being in sight of one another; 'never faced any threat' is far beyond the text. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The text reports Toussaint's argument that tower placement (facing away from routes, not intervisible, overlooking water) fits water claims better than defense. Poor construction is never claimed (towers are tall, thick-walled); warning-signaling is argued against; 'never faced any threat' overstates her claim.]
